sections.html:
• Type: Stem plant
  • Origin: North America (cultivar)
  • Growth rate: Medium
  • Height: 3 - 15+ cm

• Scientific name: Lobelia cardinalis (small submerged form, var. mini)
  • Other names: Cardinal flower, Red Cardinal, Blood-red Lobelia, Purple Lobelia, Mexican Lobelia
  • Minimum tank size: 20 litres
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Substrate: any
  • Height: 10–20 cm
  • Growth rate: slow to moderate (submersed), moderate (emersed)
  • Placement: foreground / midground
  • CO2: not needed but recommended when submersed
  • Propagation: cuttings, lateral shoots, seed (emersed)

Lobelia cardinalis, the cardinal flower, is a flowering plant in the bellflower family Campanulaceae. It is native to the Americas: Canada, the United States, Mexico, and Central America to Colombia. It was named after the Flemish botanist Matthias de L’Obel (1538–1616) and was introduced to Europe in the 1620s.

This species is found in humid areas such as streambanks, ponds, wet meadows, and marshes. It grows in rich, medium to wet soil in full sun to part shade. It forms red flowers that mature from late summer into mid-fall.

The growth is low and dense, as the plant branches willingly, even without trimming. In addition, the mini version rarely forms the long vertical shoots which otherwise characterize Lobelia cardinalis.

It is easily propagated by planting the cut shoots down into the bottom layer. Lobelia cardinalis 'Mini' becomes most compact in good light conditions and added CO2, but also thrives well without.

Sometimes plants surprise by suddenly deviating from the way they normally grow. This is called a mutation, and Lobelia cardinalis 'Mini' is a good example of this. Lobelia cardinalis 'Mini' has originated from the general production of Lobelia cardinalis. It is characterized by its beautiful light green leaves which are closer together than on the original Lobelia, and it is also significantly smaller, hence the addition 'Mini' to the name of the plant.

Emersed form: can reach 1.2 m in height. It forms scarlet flowers and develops purple tints, and grows faster than the submerged form. Leaves are dark green with purple undersides, toothed and alternate, up to 20 cm long and 5 cm broad, lanceolate to oval.

Submerged form: looks like a completely different plant. Leaves are much smaller (about 1.5 cm), light green, with clearly visible veins. The plant reaches 10–20 cm. Do not buy it for the purple colour: it only appears when grown emersed and fades to light green underwater. High light gives a bushier, more compact plant, while low light makes it sparse and slender. It is popular in Dutch aquariums (Leyden street technique) in the midground and foreground. Many daughter plants can develop from one plant and form dense, bushy growth.

Tank requirements: it can grow emersed or submerged, so it suits garden ponds, terrariums and paludariums. Any tank size can be used; 20 litres is the minimum. Temperature 16–26 °C (in the wild it tolerates down to 1 °C). pH 6.0–7.5. It tolerates but dislikes very hard water, thriving in soft to moderately hard water of 2–12 GH. It does not tolerate salinity and is not suitable for brackish tanks.

Lighting: moderate to high. Growth is greatly reduced under low light, and the plant stretches vertically. The more light, the larger and more attractive it becomes.

Substrate: emersed plants develop a strong root system reaching 30 cm deep; submerged roots are shorter and weaker. It absorbs nutrients through roots and leaves, so nutrient-rich substrates (such as ADA Amazonia) are best, but with regular fertilisation any substrate works.

CO2 and fertilisation: CO2 is optional, but the plant grows best in water rich in CO2 and nutrients, improving leaf and lateral shoot formation. It needs both micro- and macronutrients; fertilisation is a must. Liquid fertilisers give better growth than root tabs. If you keep shrimp, note that high CO2 and copper (found in most fertilisers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Planting: plant in a substrate layer of 5–7 cm. Plantlets need little spacing, and dense groupings do not hinder it. Dosing fertiliser after planting helps new shoots form faster.

Propagation: by seed (when emersed), cutting mature stems, lateral shoots near the stem base, or dividing daughter plants. You can cut the top just above a leaf, strip the lower leaves to leave 2.5–5 cm of bare stem, and plant it; the bottom produces roots and side shoots. For seeds, a dry start method works: growth appears in 5–10 days, and at 3–5 leaves the plant can be moved. It transitions well to submerged growth in high light.

Problems: crown rot can affect the plant. Stems may turn yellow and leggy; cut them off. Pond snails can eat the leaves, especially outdoors; remove snails and/or disinfect plants. Poor, slender growth is usually caused by a lack of CO2, low light, low nutrients, or a combination. All Lobelia are potentially toxic to humans and animals; Lobelia cardinalis contains toxic alkaloids including lobelamine and lobeline. Symptoms of ingesting large quantities include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, salivation, exhaustion, weakness and dilated pupils.

Benefits: a decorative addition to Dutch aquascapes; it does not overshadow other plants; it gives cover for fish, fry, shrimp and small frogs; it provides biofilm as first food for fry and shrimplets; it oxygenates the water.

Tankmates: compatible with a wide variety of freshwater fish, shrimp and snails. Do not keep with crayfish or freshwater crabs, which tear the foliage and uproot the plant. Avoid aggressive plant-eating fish such as Texas cichlids, Jack Dempsey, Red Devil and Oscars.

Buying: it is affordable and widely available. Choose fresh specimens without rips, discoloration, curls or dead stems and leaves.
